meta.title: Who really said "Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day. Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Lao Tzu. The adage was coined by English novelist Anne Thackeray Ritchie in 1885; the modern "for a lifetime" wording evolved in the 20th century.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day. Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Lao Tzu. The adage traces to Anne Thackeray Ritchie's 1885 novel Mrs. Dymond; the modern "for a lifetime" phrasing is a 20th-century evolution.

answer.label: Not Lao Tzu — actually Anne Thackeray Ritchie
answer.authorDates: 1837–1919 · English novelist & essayist, eldest daughter of W. M. Thackeray
answer.sourceLine: There is no basis for the Lao Tzu credit — the line appears in none of his works, and both Quote Investigator and Wikiquote list it as misattributed. QI traces the adage to Ritchie’s 1885 novel Mrs. Dymond (“if you give a man a fish he is hungry again in an hour. If you teach him to catch a fish you do him a good turn”); the familiar “feed him for a lifetime” wording is a later 20th-century evolution with no single authored source.

source.heading: Where the saying really comes from
source.excerpt: if you give a man a fish he is hungry again in an hour. If you teach him to catch a fish you do him a good turn.
trail: The definitive investigation is Quote Investigator, which concludes Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie “deserves credit for formulating a striking adage that used fishing as a paradigmatic task enabling self-sufficiency” in her 1885 novel Mrs. Dymond.
Wikiquote files the line under Lao Tzu’s Misattributed section, noting the origin is unknown and that it has also been wrongly credited to Confucius and Guan Zhong.
Wiktionary records it as “apparently coined by Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie in her 1885 novel Mrs. Dymond, although frequently now attributed to Laozi or other Chinese thinkers.”

QI documents the wording drifting toward the modern form — M. Loane’s 1911 The Common Growth has “teach him to catch a fish, and he will be richer all his life,” and a 1961 Illinois newspaper first pairs “feed him for a day” with “feed him for a lifetime.”
source.excerptNote: Ritchie’s original 1885 phrasing in Mrs. Dymond. The now-standard “feed him for a day … feed him for a lifetime” form developed over the following decades; a close 1961 version reads “You give a poor man a fish and you feed him for a day. You teach him to fish … that will feed him for a lifetime.”

source.rightsNote: The underlying adage originated in Anne Thackeray Ritchie’s Mrs. Dymond (1885), which is long in the public domain — but the specific popular wording asked about (“feed him for a day … feed him for a lifetime”) is not Ritchie’s. That exact form is an anonymous 20th-century evolution with no single identifiable author or source, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted for it.

author.name: Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie
author.heading: Who actually coined it
author.metaLine: 1837–1919 · English novelist & essayist, eldest daughter of W. M. Thackeray
author.bio: Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie (1837–1919) was an English novelist, memoirist and essayist, the eldest daughter of Vanity Fair author William Makepeace Thackeray. In her 1885 novel Mrs. Dymond she framed the fishing metaphor for self-sufficiency that, decades later and much rewritten, hardened into the familiar “teach a man to fish” proverb now falsely pinned on ancient sages.

misattribution.heading: How Lao Tzu got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a classic feel-good adage magnetically drawn to ancient sages. It has been pinned on half a dozen “wise Eastern” figures, but none of them wrote it.

items.why: The line appears in no text of Lao Tzu. Wikiquote lists it under Misattributed, and Quote Investigator found the claim of an old Chinese origin has “only weak support.”

items.who: Confucius, Guan Zhong, Maimonides, Mao Zedong
items.why: QI notes the adage has been variously called Chinese, Native American, Italian, Indian, or Biblical, and linked to Maimonides and Mao; Wikiquote adds Confucius and Guan Zhong. None is documented.
Wiktionary and QI agree the adage was “apparently coined by Anne Isabella Thackeray Ritchie in her 1885 novel Mrs. Dymond.”

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is a real, datable coinage — Anne Thackeray Ritchie, Mrs. Dymond, 1885 — and the exact “feed him for a lifetime” wording is a 20th-century paraphrase, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why the wording keeps drifting
lead: The proverb we know today was assembled gradually. Ritchie’s 1885 original spoke of a man “hungry again in an hour” who is done “a good turn” by learning to catch fish. By 1911 M. Loane had him “richer all his life,” and only around 1961 does a version pair “feed him for a day” against “feed him for a lifetime.”

Because the polished modern form has no single author, it became easy to hang on whichever ancient sage sounded authoritative — which is exactly how Lao Tzu, Confucius and others ended up credited for a Victorian novelist’s idea.
context.pull: A Victorian novelist’s line, slowly rewritten, then handed to an ancient sage.
